mn82:5.1: para. 5. ‘ussata’: this cannot mean ‘run away’ as given in P.T.S. Dict. See Comy.
mn82:6.1: Raṭṭhapāla waited until the others had left as he feared that relatives and friends of his family who were among the visitors, would disapprove of his wish to go forth and try to prevent it, because he was the only son of his parents. (_Comy._ quoted in _Wheel 110_, B.P.S.)
mn82:6.6: This is rule in the Vinaya. A novice must be able to answer ‘yes’ to this question during ordination.
mn82:11.8: Raṭṭhapāla’s parents are evidently so upset at his Going-forth that they give permission through his friends and do not come to see him.
mn82:12.1: This points to the fact that he had fasted for many days.
mn82:14.1: Literally 'before long'. Though the Discourse does not say how long it took Raṭṭhapāla to attain Arahantship, the Comy. informs us that it was twelve years (which to most people would be a long time). Genuine progress in Dhamma cannot be gained quickly and easily by most people. The Comy.'s figure of twelve years may be correct as the servant (see para. 22) did not recognize him at first. (Wheel 110).
mn82:16.3: This garden (possibly a deer park) had been given by the king for the use of ascetics and monks who arrived at the place too late to go to a monastery. Raṭṭhapāla did not wish to inform his parents of his arrival as he wanted to avoid any elaborate welcome, and therefore he preferred to stay for the night in that garden (Comy. in Wheel 110).
mn82:17.4: Comy: the father felt resentment against the bhikkhus because he wrongly believed that they had prevented his son from visiting his parents for so many years. (Wheel 110).
mn82:19.3: 10. According to Comy: Raṭṭhapāla’s father was so overcome by grief that he could not complete his sentence and only exclaimed: ‘Surely there is.’ He may have wanted to say: Surely there is enough food and wealth in our house, ‘and you will be eating stale porridge.’ (Wheel 110).
mn82:23.2: 11. A common idea in Indian religion is that by abstaining from sexual pleasure in this life and practising also moral restraint, one would be born in one of sensual-sphere heavens surrounded by celestial nymphs. This would be an impure life divine according to Buddha. See A. Sevens. 47. And note also one use of this bait by the Buddha for training Nanda. See Dhammapada commentary, Buddhist Legends, part I, p. 217ff.
mn82:29.1: para. 36. pārijuñña—loss: not in P.T.S. Dict.
mn82:31.9: para. 52. v.4 ‘Alas, would our kin were immortal!’ in Psalms of the Brethren, and so apparently Theragāthā Comy, but the Comy. to this Sutta says ‘amarā ti cāhūti amarā iti ca āhu idaṁ vuttaṁ hoti: yaṁ mataṁ ñātiṁ parivāretvā kandanti taṁ “Aho vata amhākaṁ bhātā mato, putto mata” ti ādīni pi vadanti’, from which it is obvious that amarā is here not taken as the nom. plur. adj. (immortal—āmarā) but the 3rd per. sing. aorist of marati (q.v. P.T.S. Dict.). Read no āmarāti not ne amarā ti with Comy.
mn82:38.5: para. 47. alamatto--sturdy: Reading is corrected in P.T.S. Dict. to alamattho; but this contradicts the Comy. which says ‘alamatto’ ti ‘samattha-attābhāvo’.
